[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Joins, Merges, and Concat Strategies in Pandas"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Combining datasets is a fundamental skill in data manipulation. Pandas provides three primary methods for combining DataFrames: concat, merge, and join. Choosing the correct strategy depends on the structural relationship between your data sources."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Concatenation using pd.concat"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Concatenation glues DataFrames together along an axis (row-wise or column-wise). It is ideal for stacking datasets that share the same columns or appending columns that share the same index."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"import pandas as pd

df1 = pd.DataFrame({'A': ['A0', 'A1'], 'B': ['B0', 'B1']})
df2 = pd.DataFrame({'A': ['A2', 'A3'], 'B': ['B2', 'B3']})

result_axis0 = pd.concat([df1, df2], axis=0)
print(result_axis0)"},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use axis=0 to stack DataFrames vertically (row-wise)."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use axis=1 to align DataFrames horizontally by their index."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use the ignore_index=True parameter to reset the index if the original indices are not meaningful."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Database-style Merging using pd.merge"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"The merge function is designed for database-style joining. It combines DataFrames based on one or more key columns, handling inner, outer, left, and right joins efficiently."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"left_df = pd.DataFrame({'key': ['K0', 'K1', 'K2'], 'val_left': [1, 2, 3]})
right_df = pd.DataFrame({'key': ['K1', 'K2', 'K3'], 'val_right': [4, 5, 6]})

merged_inner = pd.merge(left_df, right_df, on='key', how='inner')
print(merged_inner)"},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"how='inner': Returns only the rows where the keys exist in both DataFrames."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"how='left': Retains all rows from the left DataFrame, filling missing right values with NaN."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"how='outer': Performs a full outer join, keeping all rows from both datasets."},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Index-based Joining using DataFrame.join"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"The join method is a convenient wrapper around merge that relies on the index of the DataFrames rather than arbitrary columns. It is particularly useful when working with hierarchical or time-series indices."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"caller = pd.DataFrame({'A': ['A0', 'A1']}, index=['K0', 'K1'])
other = pd.DataFrame({'B': ['B0', 'B1']}, index=['K0', 'K1'])

joined_df = caller.join(other)
print(joined_df)"},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"DataFrame.join defaults to a left join on indices."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"You can pass an on parameter to join a DataFrame's index against a column in the caller."},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary and Best Practices"},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use concat for stacking homogeneous data (same schema, multiple files or chunks)."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use merge for relational data modeling (linking tables via common keys/columns)."},{"order":23,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use join when index alignment is the primary mechanism of combination."}]
